Both integrate changes. Different history shape.

## Merge

Joins two branches, makes merge commit. History show exactly what happened.

```
A---B---C  main
         \
          D---E---F  feature
               ↓ merge
A---B---C---M  main
     \     /
      D---E---F
```

## Rebase

Replants feature commits on top of main. Linear history, no merge commit.

```
A---B---C  main
         \
          D'--E'--F'  feature (replanted)
```

## When use each

**Merge:**
- Public/shared branches
- Want preserve real history
- Merging feature → main in team setting
- Safety: never rewrites commits

**Rebase:**
- Local cleanup before PR
- Want clean linear history
- Pulling main updates into personal feature branch
- Avoid "noisy" merge commits

## Tradeoffs

| | Merge | Rebase |
|--|-------|--------|
| History | Truthful, messy | Clean, linear |
| Safety | Always safe | Dangerous on shared branches |
| Conflicts | Resolve once | Resolve per commit |
| Blame/bisect | Harder | Easier |

## Golden rule

**Never rebase shared branch.** Rewrites commit hashes → breaks everyone else's history.

Safe pattern:
```bash
# Update feature branch with latest main
git checkout feature
git rebase main        # OK: only you use this branch

# Integrate to main
git checkout main
git merge feature      # or merge --no-ff to preserve branch context
```

TL;DR: rebase for clean local work, merge for shared integration.
